claim: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) is a major target of autoantibodies in myasthenia gravis (MG).
source: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) is a major target of autoantibodies in myasthenia gravis (MG), an autoimmune disease that causes neuromuscular transmission dysfunction.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by extensive citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that causes neuromuscular transmission dysfunction.
source: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) is a major target of autoantibodies in myasthenia gravis (MG), an autoimmune disease that causes neuromuscular transmission dysfunction.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the nature of MG.

claim: The crystal structure of the nAChR α1 subunit bound by the Fab fragment of mAb35 was determined at 2.61 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present the crystal structure of the nAChR α1 subunit bound by the Fab fragment of mAb35, a reference monoclonal antibody that causes experimental MG and competes with ~65% of antibodies from MG patients.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the Results section and confirmed in Supplementary file 1.

claim: mAb35 competes with approximately 65% of antibodies from MG patients.
source: Here, we present the crystal structure of the nAChR α1 subunit bound by the Fab fragment of mAb35, a reference monoclonal antibody that causes experimental MG and competes with ~65% of antibodies from MG patients.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Myasthenia gravis afflicts more than 20 in 100,000 people.
source: This receptor is also a major target of autoimmune antibodies in patients with myasthenia gravis (MG), an autoimmune disease that afflicts more than 20 in 100,000 people (Lindstrom, 2000; Vincent et al., 2001).
evidence: This prevalence statistic is directly stated with supporting citations.

claim: MG is the first and only autoimmune disease with a well-defined autoantigen target.
source: MG is the first and, so far, only autoimmune disease with well-defined autoantigen target; the binding of nAChR by MG antibodies leads to complement-mediated lysis of the postsynaptic structure and internalization of the receptor, thereby disrupting neuromuscular transmission (Engel and Arahata, 1987; Drachman et al., 1978; Gomez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the unique status of MG among autoimmune diseases.

claim: The binding of nAChR by MG antibodies leads to complement-mediated lysis of the postsynaptic structure and internalization of the receptor.
source: MG is the first and, so far, only autoimmune disease with well-defined autoantigen target; the binding of nAChR by MG antibodies leads to complement-mediated lysis of the postsynaptic structure and internalization of the receptor, thereby disrupting neuromuscular transmission (Engel and Arahata, 1987; Drachman et al., 1978; Gomez et al., 2010).
evidence: This mechanism is stated with supporting citations.

claim: More than 85% of MG patients carry nAChR antibodies.
source: In fact, more than 85% of MG patients carry nAChR antibodies (Lindstrom, 2000; Vincent et al., 2001; Meriggioli and Sanders, 2009).
evidence: This statistic is directly stated with supporting citations.

claim: The total amount of nAChR antibodies in the serum of MG patients does not correlate with disease severity.
source: However, the total amount of nAChR antibodies in the serum of MG patients does not seem to correlate with disease severity, suggesting that various nAChR antibodies that bind different regions on nAChR may contribute differently to this disease (Somnier, 1993; Berrih-Aknin, 1995; Mossman et al., 1988; Tzartos et al., 1998).
evidence: This observation is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Mammalian muscle nAChR has a pentameric structure composed of two α1, one β1, one δ, and one ε (adult form) or γ (fetal form) subunit(s).
source: Mammalian muscle nAChR has a pentameric structure composed of two α1, one β1, one δ, and one ε (adult form) or γ (fetal form) subunit(s) (Unwin, 2005).
evidence: This structural composition is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: More than half of all autoantibodies in MG and EAMG bind an overlapping region on the nAChR α1 subunit known as the main immunogenic region (MIR).
source: Furthermore, more than half of all autoantibodies in MG and EAMG bind an overlapping region on the nAChR α1 subunit, known as the main immunogenic region (MIR) (Tzartos et al., 1998).
evidence: This is directly stated with a supporting citation.

claim: mAb35 inhibits the binding of about 65% autoantibodies from MG patients or rats with EAMG.
source: The MIR is defined by the ability of a single rat monoclonal antibody (mAb), mAb35, to inhibit the binding of about 65% autoantibodies from MG patients or rats with EAMG (Tzartos and Lindstrom, 1980; Tzartos et al., 1982, 1983).
evidence: This defining characteristic of the MIR is stated with supporting citations.

claim: MIR has been mapped to a peptide region that spans residues 67–76 on nAChR α1.
source: Subsequent studies have mapped MIR to a peptide region that spans residues 67–76 on nAChR α1 (Barkas et al., 1988; Tzartos et al., 1988).
evidence: This mapping result is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies directed to the MIR can passively transfer EAMG and possess all the key pathological functions of serum autoantibodies from MG patients.
source: Monoclonal antibodies directed to the MIR can passively transfer EAMG and possess all the key pathological functions of serum autoantibodies from MG patients (Tzartos et al., 1987).
evidence: This functional characteristic is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Titer levels of MIR-specific antibody from MG patients correlate with disease severity.
source: Moreover, a recent study showed that titer levels of MIR-specific antibody from MG patients, rather than the total amount of nAChR antibodies, correlate with disease severity (Masuda et al., 2012).
evidence: This correlation is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: mAb35 binds natively folded nAChR α1 with high affinity (Kd =~2 nM).
source: Although mAb35 does not bind well to the denatured receptor, it has been shown to bind natively folded nAChR α1 with high affinity (Kd =~2 nM) (Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This binding affinity is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Crystal structures of both human and mouse nAChR α1 ECD in complex with Fab35 and α-Btx were obtained at 2.61 Å and 2.70 Å resolution, respectively.
source: We obtained ternary complex crystals with both human and mouse nAChR α1 ECD and solved the structures (2.61 Å and 2.70 Å resolution, respectively) by molecular replacement (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The resolutions of both structures are explicitly stated.

claim: The antibody/receptor interface appears identical between the human and mouse complexes.
source: A detailed comparison between the two complex structures is presented in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2. Here, we focus our structural description and analysis on the antibody/receptor interface, which appears identical between the human and mouse complexes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section.

claim: Fab35 binds to nAChR α1 in an upright orientation, away from the α-Btx.
source: The Fab35 binds to nAChR α1 in an upright orientation, away from the α-Btx (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This orientation is described in text and shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: The buried solvent accessible area of the Fab35-nAChR α1 complex is 899 Å2.
source: The Fab35 binding sites on nAChR α1 include the MIR and the N-terminal helix; the buried solvent accessible area of the complex is 899 Å2.
evidence: This quantitative measurement is stated directly.

claim: The complementarity determining regions CDR-H2, CDR-H3 from the heavy chain, and CDR-L3 from the light chain form the binding site of nAChR α1 on Fab35.
source: Fab35 has the canonical IgG antibody structure where the complementarity determining regions (CDRs) from the heavy chain, CDR-H2 and CDR-H3, and the light chain, CDR-L3, form the binding site of nAChR α1 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: The MIR loop inserts deeply into a surface pocket between the variable domains of the heavy and light chains (VH and VL) of Fab35.
source: On the receptor side (Figure 2a), the MIR loop inserts deeply into a surface pocket between the variable domains of the heavy and light chains (VH and VL), whereas the N-terminal helix sits into a groove on the surface of the heavy chain.
evidence: This structural feature is described in text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The N-terminal helix sits into a groove on the surface of the heavy chain of Fab35.
source: On the receptor side (Figure 2a), the MIR loop inserts deeply into a surface pocket between the variable domains of the heavy and light chains (VH and VL), whereas the N-terminal helix sits into a groove on the surface of the heavy chain.
evidence: This structural feature is described in text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The CDR-H3 from Fab35 inserts into a surface pocket formed by the N-terminal helix, the loop following the N-terminal helix, the MIR and the loop preceding the MIR on nAChR α1.
source: On the Fab35 side (Figure 2b), the CDR-H3 inserts into a surface pocket formed by the N-terminal helix, the loop following the N-terminal helix, the MIR and the loop preceding the MIR.
evidence: This structural feature is described in text and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The nAChR α1 structure remains the same in the ternary Fab35/nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx complex and the binary nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx complex.
source: Superposition of the structures of mouse nAChR α1 ECD in the ternary Fab35/nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx complex with that in the binary nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx complex (PDB ID, 2QC1) (Dellisanti et al., 2007a) shows that the nAChR α1 structure remains the same in the two complex states (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This comparison is stated in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Fab35 recognizes and binds a well-defined and preformed conformation of the nAChR α1 ECD.
source: This structural comparison suggests that Fab35 recognizes and binds a well-defined and preformed conformation of the nAChR α1 ECD.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the structural comparison data.

claim: Four 'hotspot' residues on nAChR α1 that make numerous contacts to Fab35 were identified: Asn68 and Asp71 from the MIR loop and Arg6 and Lys10 from the N-terminal helix.
source: The contacting analysis also revealed several residues on nAChR α1 that make numerous contacts to Fab35. Four such 'hotspots' of binding were identified: Asn68 and Asp71 from the MIR loop and Arg6 and Lys10 from the N-terminal helix.
evidence: These hotspot residues are identified from the structural analysis.

claim: Asp71 forms a salt bridge with Arg50 of VH and a hydrogen bond with Tyr95 of VL.
source: Asp71 forms a salt bridge with Arg50 of VH and a hydrogen bond with Tyr95 of VL (Figure 3a).
evidence: These specific interactions are described in text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The amide group of Asn68 side chain forms three hydrogen bonds with VL (the carbonyl of Tyr91 main chain and the amide and carbonyl of Gly94 main chain).
source: At Asn68, another hotspot site (Figure 3b), the amide group of Asn68 side chain forms three hydrogen bonds with VL (the carbonyl of Tyr91 main chain and the amide and carbonyl of Gly94 main chain).
evidence: These specific hydrogen bonds are described in text and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The guanidinium head group of Arg6 forms bidentate hydrogen bonds with Asp54 and cation-π stacking with Trp52 of VH.
source: The guanidinium head group of Arg6 forms bidendate hydrogen bonds with Asp54 and cation-π stacking with Trp52 of VH.
evidence: These specific interactions are described in the text.

claim: Lys10 forms salt bridges with Asp53 of VH.
source: Lys10 forms salt bridges with Asp53 of VH (Figure 3c); its side chain also makes van der Waals contacts to numerous VH residues (not shown).
evidence: This interaction is described in text and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Fab35 and Fab198 share a conserved immunoglobulin fold and a similar antigen-binding site.
source: Interestingly, superposition of the structure of Fab198 onto that of Fab35 in the ternary complex shows that these two Fabs share not only a conserved immunoglobulin fold but also a similar antigen-binding site (Figure 4a).
evidence: This structural similarity is described in text and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Many key α1-binding residues in Fab35 are conserved in Fab198 and appear to make similar contacts to nAChR α1 in the modeled Fab198/nAChR α1 binding interface.
source: Even more remarkably, many key α1-binding residues in Fab35 are also conserved in Fab198 and they appear to make similar contacts to nAChR α1 in the modeled Fab198/nAChR α1 binding interface (Figure 4a and c).
evidence: This conservation is described in text and shown in Figures 4a and 4c.

claim: The CDR-H3 loops between Fab198 and Fab35 differ significantly in length and sequence.
source: However, in contrast to the above structural similarities, the CDR-H3 loops between Fab198 and Fab35 differ significantly in length and sequence (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This difference is described in text and shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claim: mAb35 and mAb198 share a high similarity in binding mechanism to the core MIR/N-terminal helix region, but differ in the periphery of the binding interface.
source: These structural analyses suggest that mAb35 and mAb198 share a high similarity in binding mechanism to the core MIR/N-terminal helix region, but differ in the periphery of the binding interface.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the structural comparison.

claim: Fab192 differs significantly from Fab35 in terms of their binding mechanisms to nAChR α1.
source: This structural comparison suggests that Fab192 differs significantly from Fab35 in terms of their binding mechanisms to nAChR α1, confirming and extending the differences that were previously recognized between mAb35 and mAb192 (Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from structural comparison and supported by a citation.

claim: Fab35 binds specifically to nAChR α1 but not α9.
source: Consistent with the above structural analyses, we have shown by native PAGE that Fab35 indeed binds specifically to nAChR α1 but not α9 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This binding specificity is demonstrated experimentally by native PAGE shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Fab35-binding residues are conserved in nAChR α1 across a wide range of species.
source: For the second part of the question, a similar structure-based sequence comparison shows that Fab35-binding residues are conserved in nAChR α1 across a wide range of species (Figure 5d), which is consistent with the high cross-reactivity of autoantibodies in MG and EAMG between different species (Tzartos et al., 1998, 1982; Luo et al., 2009; Gomez et al., 1981).
evidence: This conservation is shown in Figure 5d and supported by citations.

claim: Xenopus nAChR α1 does not bind Fab35.
source: Consistent with these structural observations, previous studies have shown that Xenopus nAChR α1 indeed does not bind Fab35 (Saedi et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Fab35, by binding to the extruding tip of an α1 subunit, makes no direct contact to the neighboring subunits in the nAChR pentamer.
source: This model suggests that Fab35, by binding to the extruding tip of an α1 subunit, makes no direct contact to the neighboring subunits.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling analysis.

claim: Fab35 binds nAChR α1 at a site that is far away from the ligand-binding site.
source: Moreover, Fab35 binds nAChR α1 at a site that is far away from the ligand-binding site, consistent with the observation that MIR-directed antibodies generally do not affect the channel function (Tzartos et al., 1981; Gomez et al., 1981; Tamamizu et al., 1996).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by citations.

claim: The two Fabs from a single mAb35 antibody are unable to bind to the two α1 subunits within the same nAChR pentamer due to steric and geometric constraints.
source: After putting all of the molecular components on proper scale and orientation, our model of the full-length antibody/receptor complex suggests that, as a result of steric and geometric constraints, the two Fabs from a single mAb35 antibody are unable to bind to the two α1 subunits within the same nAChR pentamer (Figure 6c).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: MG antibodies will bind two α1 subunits from different pentamers, thereby cross-linking the nAChRs.
source: Consequently, MG antibodies will bind two α1 subunits from different pentamers, thereby cross-linking the nAChRs.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling analysis.

claim: The modeling analyses are consistent with previous sucrose density gradient studies showing that mAb35 and similar mAbs cannot bind the two α1 subunits within the same pentamer but can cross-link adjacent nAChR pentamers.
source: Our modeling analyses are consistent with previous sucrose density gradient studies showing that mAb35 and similar mAbs cannot bind the two α1 subunits within the same pentamer but can cross-link adjacent nAChR pentamers (Conti-Tronconi et al., 1981).
evidence: The modeling results are validated by comparison with previous experimental studies.

claim: The binding of nAChR by the divalent MG antibodies rather than the monovalent Fab fragment leads to accelerated degradation of the receptor proteins.
source: Previous studies have shown that the binding of nAChR by the divalent MG antibodies rather than the monovalent Fab fragment leads to accelerated degradation of the receptor proteins (Drachman et al., 1978).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Cross-linking of the nAChRs is a critical step in receptor degradation.
source: This observation suggests that cross-linking of the nAChRs is a critical step in receptor degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation about divalent vs. monovalent antibody effects.

claim: Receptor cross-linking is an intrinsic property of mAb35 and mAb35-like MG antibodies.
source: Our analyses suggest that receptor cross-linking is an intrinsic property of mAb35 and mAb35-like MG antibodies.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and modeling analyses.

claim: The crystal structure provides the first atomic view of the detailed interactions between an EAMG antibody and the nAChR.
source: Our crystal structure of Fab35 bound to the nAChR α1 ECD provides the first atomic view of the detailed interactions between an EAMG antibody and the nAChR.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: The N-terminal helix (residues 1–14) is important for high-affinity MG antibody binding.
source: More recent studies using natively folded nAChR α1/α7 chimera proteins (Luo et al., 2009) or GFP-fused protein fragments (Morell et al., 2014) showed that the N-terminal helix (residues 1–14) is also important for high-affinity MG antibody binding.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Asn68 and Asp71 of MIR are essential for MG antibody binding.
source: These studies showed that Asn68 and Asp71 of MIR are essential for MG antibody binding while the surrounding residues including Pro69 and Tyr72 showed partial effect when mutated.
evidence: This is stated based on previous mutational studies.

claim: Arg6 and Lys10 on the N-terminal helix are critical to MG antibody binding.
source: On the N-terminal helix of Torpedo nAChR α1, two exposed residues, Arg6 and Asn10, which correspond to Arg6 and Lys10 in human nAChR α1, respectively, are found to be critical to MG antibody binding by mutational analyses (Morell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Many MIR-directed antibodies may share high similarities in their binding sites on the nAChR.
source: Although biochemical mapping of antibody-binding residues on nAChR α1 were performed with different antibodies (e.g. mAb210 and mAb132A) (Barkas et al., 1988; Tzartos et al., 1988; Das and Lindstrom, 1989; Saedi et al., 1990; Papadouli et al., 1990, 1993; Luo et al., 2009; Morell et al., 2014), it is remarkable that these biochemical data agree so well with our crystal structure, suggesting that many MIR-directed antibodies may share high similarities in their binding sites on the nAChR.
evidence: This is inferred from the agreement between the crystal structure and previous biochemical data.

claim: Molecular mimicries of the MIR and its immediate surrounding regions could be developed to bind a significant fraction of MIR-directed MG autoantibodies.
source: An important implication of this finding is that molecular mimicries of the MIR and its immediate surrounding regions could be developed to bind a significant fraction of MIR-directed MG autoantibodies.
evidence: This is a speculative implication drawn from the structural findings.

claim: The complete epitope for mAb35 consists of two separated peptide regions (the MIR loop and the N-terminal helix) that are required to fold together properly for optimal binding.
source: Most MIR-directed mAbs, such as mAb35, bind preferably to folded receptors. Our structure shows that the complete epitope consists of two separated peptide regions (the MIR loop and the N-terminal helix) that are required to fold together properly for optimal binding.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural analysis.

claim: The native conformation of the MIR that permits binding of mAbs 35 and 198 depends on the interaction of the N-terminal helix with the MIR loop.
source: These structural observations are consistent with previous studies of chimeras and mutants showing that the native conformation of the MIR that permits binding of mAbs 35 and 198 depends on the interaction of the N-terminal helix with the MIR loop (Luo et al., 2009; Dellisanti et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Neighboring subunits in the nAChR pentamer do not make direct contact to Fab35.
source: Our modeling analyses indicate that neighboring subunits in the nAChR pentamer do not make direct contact to Fab35, suggesting that the binding interactions observed in our crystal structures represent most, if not all, of those in the native complexes between mAb35 and the full-length nAChR pentamer.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling analysis.

claim: Antibodies in MG serum and mAbs bind mature and pentameric nAChR more tightly than the unassembled nAChR α1 monomer.
source: However, it is known that antibodies in MG serum and mAbs bind mature and pentameric nAChR more tightly than the unassembled nAChR α1 monomer (Luo et al., 2009; Merlie and Lindstrom, 1983; Conroy et al., 1990), and there is evidence that MIR plays an important role in initiating conformational maturation of subunits prior to their assembly into pentameric AChR receptors (Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Some MG mAbs bind neuronal nAChR subunits.
source: Consistent with this notion, it has been shown that some MG mAbs bind neuronal nAChR subunits. mAb35 was shown to bind chicken nAChR α3 and also suggested to bind human α2, α3, α5 and β3 (Conroy and Berg, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: mAb210 has been used to bind human α5 and β3.
source: Another MIR-directed antibody, mAb210, has been used to bind human α5 and β3 (Kuryatov et al., 2008; Wang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: MG antibodies are unlikely to bind two nAChR pentamers oriented vertically on a flat membrane surface even when considering the hinge flexibility of the antibody.
source: We further noticed that MG antibodies are unlikely to bind two nAChR pentamers oriented vertically on a flat membrane surface even when considering the hinge flexibility of the antibody (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A potential effect of antibody-mediated receptor cross-linking is membrane curvature.
source: Assuming that the nAChR pentamers in the membrane cannot be tilted freely, a potential effect of antibody-mediated receptor cross-linking is membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: Molecular mimicries of the MIR should prevent cross-linking and degradation of nAChR by competitive binding to MG antibodies.
source: While the detailed mechanisms by which antibody-mediated receptor cross-linking induces the receptor degradation remain to be elucidated, molecular mimicries of the MIR should prevent such cross-linking and degradation of nAChR by competitive binding to MG antibodies (Sophianos and Tzartos, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: It is possible to develop drug molecules to inhibit the binding of a large fraction of MG antibodies to nAChR and related pathological immune reactions.
source: Our studies suggest that it is possible to develop drug molecules to inhibit the binding of a large fraction of MG antibodies to nAChR and related pathological immune reactions, and the crystal structures presented here provide a basis for developing such drug molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative implication drawn from the structural findings.

claim: The α211 construct contains three point mutations (V8E, W149R, and V155A) for improved solubility and stability.
source: The construct was truncated at the 211th amino acid from the N-terminal of nAChR α1 subunit without a signal sequence, and three point mutations (V8E, W149R, and V155A) were introduced for improved solubility and stability (Dellisanti et al., 2007a; Chen, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: Crystals of the ternary complex were grown in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate trihydrate, pH 6.5, 0.1–0.15 M calcium acetate hydrate and 18–20% (w/v) PEG 8K.
source: The optimized condition was 0.1 M sodium cacodylate trihydrate, pH 6.5, 0.1–0.15 M calcium acetate hydrate and 18–20% (w/v) PEG 8K.
evidence: This crystallization condition is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Both human and mouse complex crystals belong to the space group C2.
source: Both human and mouse complex crystals belong to the space group C2, with unit cell dimensions of a = 160.0 Å, b = 42.1 Å, c = 136.5 Å, β = 117.1°; and a = 159.9 Å, b = 42.0 Å, c = 137.6 Å, β = 116.5°, respectively.
evidence: This crystallographic information is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The crystal structures were solved by molecular replacement using PHASER MR.
source: The crystal structures were solved by molecular replacement using PHASER MR (McCoy et al., 2007) in CCP4 (Collaborative Computational Project Number 4, 1994) and the coordinates of α211/α-Btx complex (PDB ID, 2QC1) and Fab198 (PDB ID, 1FN4, modified to poly-Ala) (Dellisanti et al., 2007a; Poulas et al., 2001).
evidence: This method is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The human nAChR α1 ECD appears very similar to the previously characterized mouse nAChR α1 ECD.
source: Our study also generated the first atomic picture of the human nAChR α1 ECD, which appears very similar to the previously characterized mouse nAChR α1 ECD (PDB ID, 2QC1) (Lindstrom, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption.

claim: A significant structural difference between the human and mouse nAChR α1 ECDs is the binding interface of α-Btx.
source: A significant structural difference between the human and mouse nAChR α1 ECDs is the binding interface of α-Btx.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption.

claim: In the mouse nAChR α1 ECD, Phe189 is inserted into a surface pocket of α-Btx.
source: In the mouse nAChR α1 ECD, Phe189 is inserted into a surface pocket of α-Btx.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: In the human nAChR α1 ECD, Thr189 is too small to fill in the α-Btx pocket.
source: In the human nAChR α1 ECD, Thr189, is too small to fill in the α-Btx pocket.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: The observations about Phe189 and Thr189 are consistent with predictions from previous analyses of the nAChR α1/α-Btx complex.
source: These observations are consistent with predictions from previous analyses of the nAChR α1/α-Btx complex (Vincent et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption with a supporting citation.

claim: Coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank under accession codes PDB: 5HBT (Fab35/human nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx) and 5HBV (Fab35/mouse nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx).
source: Coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank under accession codes PDB: 5HBT (Fab35/human nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx) and 5HBV (Fab35/mouse nAChR α1 ECD/α-Btx).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
